title: Autistic coding in Poor Things and the importance of representation

commenti.body:
Interesting

I didnt link any of her behavior to neurodivergence/autistic coding but that of someone who is a child.

I have a 1 year old nephew and her behavior at the beginning is identical to his - even the killing of bugs
I also read it that way.

You are correct in that the infantile brain and the results of it are representing actions of a child, from spitting out food to the erratic movement patterns.

And yet these can also apply to autistic individuals: food can be troublesome due to textures, flavors, etc, and autistic people are known to walk on their toes, pigeon toed, have unique gaits, etc

Oh I 100% agree

But just because you can link that behavior to that of someone who is autistic doesn't mean the Director has a "responsibility to raise awareness"

I think the point my girlfriend made was this wasn’t just a similarity, it was a direct representation. The story arc is that of an autistic individual learning about masking and the necessity to hide their true selves in an effort to conform to society

just because she felt that aspects of the character or plot resonated with her experience doesn't mean that that resonation was intentional by the film's creators. it just happens with art. it's great when it does, but it doesn't mean they were intentionally or consciously making a film that they knew would resonate with people with autism. there are plenty of non-autistic people that would resonate with a character feeling they need to hide their true self. it's a pretty common experience.

You can apply whatever lens you want when dissecting a film, but that in no way means that was the director’s intent unless they’ve specifically said so, no matter how abstract and open ended the story is. Even this interruption is correct (strongly feel that it isn’t) there is absolutely no point in asking a director like Lanthimos to come out and specify the exact meaning or “coding” of their films as it would alienate any other viewers who rightfully will have their own different interruptions of the story and her character and bring their own experiences to their viewing.

> The story arc is that of an autistic individual learning about masking and the necessity to hide their true selves in an effort to conform to society

I guess I would disagree with that interpretation

Where is it shown in the film that she is "masking her true self"?

Her arc is more about discovery and learning how the world works (both in good & bad ways) I didn't read her behavior at the end of the film as her hiding or conforming to society at all

I would say in short a movie like Poor Things is an artistic exploration and not a PSA. So no responsibility. The only caveat I make on that is if it’s based on the story of people who are still alive and uses real names. 

Art is definitely adopted by different groups because the people resonate with an explicit message or a vibe they feel from the movie. The classic example is Rocky Horror. But then you have the flip side. American Psycho and Fight Club critique toxic masculinity but toxic dudes often really love those moves. 

For Poor Things, I do think the neurodivergent argument is interesting. But I read her early behavior as what I’d expect from a kid. And that the laughs were because we’re watching Emma Stone acting as a child. Rather than laughing at someone who is neurodivergent.

It’s a bit complicated because there’s the literal level and the metaphoric level. The literal level is just that Bella is a child growing into this body. The metaphoric level can include the neurodivergent reading. Some people will focus more on the literal, others in the metaphorical. 

What you’re asking is essentially about how explicit movies need to be with their metaphors and the relationship between artist intentionality and audience response. 

By that last part, I mean something like… 2001: A Space Odyssey is about humanity’s relationship with technology and how it’s shaped us. That’s the intention. But people can read all kinds of things from it. Like it reminds me of my mom because she loved Arthur C Clarke. You could compare and contrast to other movies, like the feeling you get from 2001 compared to Mulholland Drive. Then you could put the movie through other frames. As a coming of age story. Or what it says about conflict or politics. Or exploring the gender dichotomy in the film. Or the absence of romance/sexuality. 

Kubrick probably didn’t intend much of those talking points. But you can use the film as a foundation for them.

Did Yorgos intend Poor Things to have neurodivergent coding? Maybe? Does he have to make that explicit? Nope. Can someone make a thoughtful interpretation of the movie through that lens—10000%
Thank you for taking the time to respond. A lot of great points in your comment.

Yup. If anything you could read her as an allegory of obtaining enlightenment. They even reference goethe and madame of the brothel spoke about how Bella the necessity of knowing the darker aspects of life. Never did I feel she masking, if anything she was calling out the absurdities of other people’s masks.

No, a filmmaker does not have a responsibility to validate any particular reading of the film. That's up to you! You found lots of evidence in the text to make a strong argument for your reading. For me, I'm doubtful of any one-for-one analogy. I have a distaste for allegory myself and am warry of any story that tries to be or analysis that tries to claim allegory or a one-for-one analog.  But, you do have an interesting take. You've expressed yourself well and presented evidence to back your claim of the text. That's great! But, no Lanthimos has no responsibility to say, "yes, you're right!"

Yeah I completely disagree with you. They perform surgery to put a baby human’s brain in an adult skull/body not once, but twice. It has nothing to do with neurodivergence and everything to do with neuro-underdevelopment and then showing the brain slowly mature into its new body and go through stages of mental development as the movie goes on. In fact, they also explicitly say this in the movie (a very important part too as Max initially calls her a “pretty retard” before knowing the truth) and documenting that development is the whole reason the Max character is introduced. 

I understand that having an autistic girlfriend probably centers your life a bit more around autism and neurodivergence in general, but not everything can be related back to that, this movie being an example of that.

Thanks for sharing and kicking off this discussion, it's really interesting.

\> if art is allowed to exist without comparisons to reality and can be adopted by any groups to be used for whatever purpose.

My take is that good art may evoke all kinds of metaphors and feelings including and beyond what the original creators intended. That isn't "allowing art to exist without comparisons to reality," it's allowing art to contain multiple layers of meaning, including the meaning that the audience members bring to it. 

I did read Bella as autistically coded; I also read her as representing the experience of girlhood in a predatory/patriarchal world. I think these are all part of the film. I imagine there are twenty other metaphors that other audience members may have read into it, and I'm excited to see those. I don't particularly need or want the filmmakers to tell us, "Oh actually, we didn't mean any of that, we actually intended it as a queer metaphor" or whatever.

This was my view when speaking to my girlfriend. The minute you define art as something, you eliminate the endless interpretations that may follow.

Her counter was that the character shared so many autistic traits, and the infant brain in a full body is such a direct metaphor for neuro developmental disorders, that it effectively surpasses an interpretation and enters a direct representation.

She feels that autistic representation on film is still a far ways away from where it should be, and having a story such as this not be given the definition it may have takes away the possible validation an autistic viewer may have. 

Her opinion, I’m merely the microphone. Thanks for commenting
I’m merely the microphone for my girlfriends experience. In any case thanks for contributing to the conversation

Interesting, what would better representation have looked like, to her? Like someone in the film directly calling Bella neurodivergent? Or just the filmmakers coming out and stating that's what they intended?

Downvotes don’t matter, it was worth the post to get a few interesting threads out of it.

For her, all she was looking for is some sort of acknowledgment either from yorgos or Emma stone that the early stages of Bella were modeled after a neurodivergent experience, because according to her it’s impossible to have that many direct similarities without it being inspired by the autistic experience. 

The slur line, in my opinion, was actually great in that it shows the startling first impression a developmental disorder can have on someone not typically exposed to it, almost like the audiences first impression to Bella

You’re coming into the film with that idea already in your head and then confirming your own bias. Nothing in the film is explicitly about autism decently not “direct representation”. It’s like a fanboy who comes up with their own fan theory and the gets annoyed the creator hasn’t somehow validated them in their exact way. Besides she doesn’t “mask” anything she begins as a child and then genuinely changes and grows up.

I understand your girlfriend's point of view, and I definitely am always seeking representation out there wherever I can for the things society has sometimes judged me for (weight, CP, etc.).

But to me her POV is also the very antithesis of what art is meant to be.

The movie doesn't belong to your girlfriend, or to any one person, and she certainly has no right to demand that the filmmakers or actress speak out and proclaim that it is exactly what she wants it to be.

Instead I really would ask her to flip the formula. Instead of being furious, hurt, and upset at the filmmakers, why doesn't she just take what she got from it as a gift, anyway? Why not try to be happy at how the film spoke to her, at how she felt it represented her own journey?

That would be so much easier, and add positivity and inclusiveness to her feelings about the movie instead of all this unnecessary entitlement. The movie is hers already, just like it belongs to every other viewer -- if it made her feel seen, she should cherish that instead of throwing tantrums or making impossible demands of artists who may have had other goals in mind to begin with (in which case, their rigidly defining their approaches or goals would only upset her further).

I hope it helps.

I think to word her better, she was arguing that the story itself wasn’t autistic, but the character displayed autistic traits, which isn’t arguable. So mainly, she just feels frustrated that autistic traits are often used to make a character feel quirky, or eccentric for an audience.

But ofc you are right, art belongs to the masses and any individual can pull from it what they want. Thank you for taking the time to add to the conversation

>but **the character displayed autistic traits, which isn’t arguable**. So mainly, she just feels frustrated that autistic traits are often used to make a character feel quirky, or eccentric for an audience.

Boldfacing mine for emphasis.

Respectfully, you're again stating an opinion as fact. *Are* they exclusively autistic traits, though? No. They aren't.

**She** feels the traits are "inarguably" autistic. I don't. Yes, I saw some behaviors that I've seen in friends with who are neurodivergent, yes, but I also saw a ton of universal human childlike, learned, and just plain wonderfully awkward behaviors that resonated with me powerfully and personally. 

I am not neurodivergent, but I was born with mild cerebral palsy, I am a geek and a misfit, so plenty of what you and she are describing in this sort of ironclad way, as "only" belonging to those who are neurodivergent, I feel is restrictive and unnecessarily excluding -- she is trying to appropriate something **that speaks to a wider audience than just her**. Again, what she sees or empathizes with doesn't belong to her alone.

Plenty of people can see themselves in Bella and that is not taking a thing away from those in the autistic or neurodivergent community.

Thank you for the conversation, and I hope this helps clarify my POV.

It definitely does, and I appreciate the well articulated points. I’m glad you found the film interesting, and we’re willing to engage in discourse surrounding it. Have a good day, and watch more great film

Thank you for the discussion, and I do hope your GF feels better.

And happy holidays, if they are taking place wherever you are!
[removed]

Perhaps Lanthimos draws some inspiration from autistic people in order to create his characters, but I don't think his films are meant to raise awareness or educate people about this particular condition. I think his films are less specific and more open to free interpretation.
[removed]

> that the early stages of Bella were modeled after a neurodivergent experience, because according to her it’s impossible to have that many direct similarities without it being inspired by the autistic experience.

What are all the direct similarities?  Has your gf ever raised a baby/toddler?

As an autistic woman, I sincerely agree with your gf. The consistent juxtaposition of what society expects of Bella versus what is within her own mind and heart was beautifully told. The frustration and confusion she experiences when encountering the competing ideologies was so personal to me. 

For allistic people, it’s a very enthralling and informative way of helping them comprehend the autistic experience and how alienating it can be to live life with the processing differences we have. My partner (allistic 32M) had leaned over multiple times in the first hour to comment on specific expressions, behaviors, and logic that Bella displays that are clearly autistic coded.

oh, are you neurodivergent and/or autistic? her behavior at the beginning is like that bc her brain exactly that, the developing level of a toddler. but she obviously doesn’t stay that way. did you not finish the movie?

When has representation ever alienated someone from enjoying or relating to a story? There are countless stories told from a male perspective or an indigenous perspective or a neurotypical perspective I’ve seen and I’ve never felt alienated when a character is clearly identified by a trait. What a terribly narrow lens you have.

The amount of comments on this thread from allistic people expressing annoyance, disgust, or dismissiveness at the idea that a character is autistic coded is so disheartening. Genuinely, to all of you getting offended by the implication, tell me you hate disability without telling me. 

It’s upsetting to get so excited about a movie and see that other autistic people agree with you only to have wholly ignorant, ableist comments posted over and over again. Does anyone think about anything other than their own egos?

OP, 

this is beside the point of your post, but your post sounds eerily similar to the experience described by an autistic insta content creator who described seeing this movie with her boyfriend! I can't help but wonder if you two are connected

Where did I say she stays that way?

And why are you so angry?

You literally made one comparison which was in the first fifteen minutes of the movie. Don’t project emotions at me, it’s take more than a confidently ignorant comment from a halfwit to make me more than annoyed.

That’s very funny, if the Instagram influencer is autisticthrifter than these are one in the same!

I was a film major and film is my field of interest, so I wanted to post it on a more film centric forum to see how the responses differed from the ones she received on her post. I find it interesting how the two echo chambers function completely different: hers sides with her experience and that of autistic representation, and the this one leans more with the director and their freedom of creating characters without a regard from real life inspirations.

Very interesting. In any case thank you for following and supporting my girlfriend’s work!
Thank you for taking the time to give your opinion, like any place on the internet echo chambers create unsafe discourse that I was trying to avoid here

I understand your frustration. If I may, and if you are on Instagram, my girlfriend has a small influencer page called autisticthrifter that may be a better environment for you to find likeminded people who aren’t as allistic

Yep, indeed, autisticthrifter it is! that's so cool. 

As for your curiosity, my quick thoughts flowing through my fingertips without too much thought (because I could take forever weighing in on every side and often have a hard time deciding, so I am going with the impulse writing): 

I can appreciate both sides of the debate about which you're gathering our thoughts. At least right now, I think ultimately the viewer/reader/listener of any art is going to take with them what resonates the most. I also think that within reason an artist—be they director, actor, musician, visual artist, dancer, author (because questions regarding artist freedom and license, interpretation, and representation, among others, dwell within the work of all of these)—needs artistic freedom and license. Otherwise, it's censored by those who would have the artist do their bidding (this seems harsh but it's the logical implication of the idea that an artist should do certain things). 

In the case of neurodivergent coding as with many instances of representation, there's a teaching moment to be had, but maybe the director shouldn't be the one forced to take on that role. If that's the case, then it ceases to actually be their art. If they choose to do so, that's a different story. Just as that goes, I think viewers shouldn't be forced to accept only the artist(s)' view but rather be given the freedom to explore the possibilities they see.

I see the teaching moment, or the bridge between the two views, so to speak, coming in with people like autisticthrifter who share their experience. While the director may have a greater audience in some ways, people aren't going to be really persuaded to think about it too much. And maybe some people will be saying that he shouldn't be talking about coding because it isn't his place (I could really see the shitstorm this could be--pardon my language). But while autisticthrifter and other folks are sharing their views, fewer people are listening and thinking on it, comparing their thoughts, but those fewer people are also heavily paying attention and sharing their views (even if only amongst friends and family). This spreads and spreads. This is how hearts and minds are changed. 

Sorry that was so much and so long (i'm a philosopher, an artist, musician, and academic/scholarly writer, so yeah eeeeeps eek), not well said, but hopefully the gist is there.

This was a fun read. You are a great writer. Thanks for taking the time to respond and try and gather both sides into one write up.

I agree with most of the points you made, and I think like you said, the most important thing is for strong voices from groups to rise up and create discourse about representation, accommodations, etc

>The story arc is that of an autistic individual learning about masking and the necessity to hide their true selves in an effort to conform to society

Couldn't you argue that's what everyone does that in a normative society. Queer people mask their queerness, people of color often need to act "respectable" to white norms, and that's a form of masking. A society that centers conformity will have masking in both neurodivergent and neurotypical people.

I’m grateful for the thought in many of the responses. 
I’m a doctor, with dual qualifications in the clinical use of film.
My professional opinion is: 
autists are severely compromised by society. They have statistically far higher rates of being victims of sexual and physical abuse, rape, Hate Crime, Mate Crime, bullying, and neglect. They do not have equitable access to education, social enrichment, sports, and the arts. The average life expectancy of an autist in the UK is only 39, in the USA it’s 36.5 yrs of age. 
For many of these reasons, suicide is at a rate 9 times higher than that of the neurotypical population.
Film is probably the most accessible art form after music. Film makers are intelligent, feeling, thoughtful humans. 
With the severe risks to autists being largely unknown to the neurotypical population, it’s important that just as some films educate about issues such as racism, the same is done for ableism. 
When ‘The Matrix’ was revealed as an allegory for the makers’ experiences of gender, it made many fans of the film think about an issue in more depth.
Wherever there is coding (prevalent in Sci-Fi in particular, but often Horror and thrillers, too) we often take pause when we learn about the representations that are coded, or even when filmmakers (Tim Burton is a good example) report they didn’t consciously code, but a community has flagged it to them, and they see it and are happy to talk about it in interviews.

Anything that builds kindness and understanding is a positive force and an opportunity to be seized.

Unfortunately modern film seems to frequently use ableism as a tool for laughs, in a way that would not be tolerated for racism or homophobia. And then these films (and TV series) gain accolades, e.g. ‘Three Bilboards’ (Google disabled viewers shame when watching this in cinemas) ‘Manchester By The Sea’, ‘Euphoria’, ‘The Bear’ etc etc etc.). One brief survey of ‘Does The Dog Die?’ reveals just how many films use anti-autsitic references as a ‘joke’ and ableist slurs as everyday parlance. 

Autsitic people lead very difficult, inequitable, targeted, lives. It isn’t ‘trendy’ to support them, and also intersectionality is glaringly absent. 

Whether it was the intended purpose to code or a happenstance that it resonates so strongly, it would be really worthwhile if anyone involved in that process - from actor to director to producer - could acknowledge this resonance, for therein the start of empathic conversation lies.
[removed]

Best response here! Sadly, we still have far to go when it comes to racism in film—look at the fraught discussions surrounding the two Avatar films, for example. And yes, ableism lags far behind the progress we’ve made with other “isms” in art, and the current discourse doesn’t allow disabled people to confidently say, “Hey, you’re portraying my lived experience and here’s how I feel about it.” Too many people dismiss it and minimize it.

Thanks so much. Completely agree, and wish I hadn’t fired off my OP but instead edited it for clarity. 
There really is a palpable dismissal of the disabled perspective, and it would be superb if this became more widely recognised, and the hardship and threats faced by autists, and other disabled groups, were more widely recognised. 
Thank you very much.

honestly i had a similar reaction when the film began, i went in blind and thought it might be a film related to autism when she was exhibiting this mismatch between body and brain but the film goes on to explain that this was due to a childs brain being transplanted into an adult body, so i read the rest of the film through that lens, as thats the exposition it tells us. just because bella’s behaviors parallel some autistic behaviors doesnt mean it’s necessarily coded, since theres a very wide range of autistic experiences, i think it would be disingenuous to say that this was the purpose of the film or this is the proper representation especially when that wasnt the original intention or explanation of the behavior that we are given

I'm autistic and I related to Bella Baxter. I think it's easy to connect what happens in the movie to the autistic experience (some autistic experiences) and it's also amazing that a movie like this was made. However, objectively speaking I do think this film is whatever the filmmaker intended it to be and once it reaches the theater it flows freely and can be interpreted and embraced by everyone in different ways. It's great that Bella represents some autistic experiences, but it's also great that allistic people can interpret it differently. That's the greatness of cinema.
